beats.text: Long before the British arrived, northern Australia was already part of an international trade network.
Every year, fleets from Makassar, in today's Indonesia, sailed over a thousand kilometres south across the Arafura Sea.
They came for sea cucumber. Dried, it was a delicacy in China, and worth the voyage.
They rode the monsoon down in December, and the same winds home months later.
On the Arnhem Land coast they built camps, boiling and drying the catch for the journey back.
But this coast wasn't empty. Aboriginal communities had lived here for tens of thousands of years, and they traded too: for metal, cloth and tools. Some sailed back to Makassar.
The traces remain. Indonesian words in Aboriginal languages. Tamarind trees at old camps. Bark paintings of the ships.
In 1803, Matthew Flinders met six of these vessels. The last recorded voyage was 1907.
Australia's history didn't begin in 1788. It was already underway, across the sea to the north.
